newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria goes off-line as net smut war heats up.
newsitem.headline: Austria goes off-line as net smut war heats up.

text.p: Austrian internet access providers vowed to take the entire country off-line for two hours on Tuesday to protest against an unprecedented move by the government to keep smut out of the worldwide computer net.

"Some 95 percent of Austrian providers which are connected internationally will take part in the protest. And more are joining us every hour," Peter Rastl of the Austrian Association of Internet Providers (ISPA) told Reuters.
Most internet services from and to Austria would be shut down between 4 p.m and 6 p.m (1600-1800 GMT), he said.

The action was sparked by a dawn raid on Vienna-based provider VIPnet last week. Police impounded the group's entire computer network on Thursday following allegations that it had been misused to feed child pornography into the net.

The raid followed a legal complaint filed by a user with German authorities in March 1996 which was later passed on to Austrian investigators. The charge was not lodged against VIPnet but against one of its clients who allegedly fed the illegal material into the internet using VIPnet's access points.
"This shockingly incompetent procedure of the authorities should be of concern to all Austrian computer users," ISPA said in a statement.

The association said policemen had pulled the plugs on VIPnet's computers without shutting them down first, which could seriously damage the machines, and took away all of its computers, pushing the company to the brink of financial ruin.

The move came amid growing alarm among governments worldwide over the darker side of the net as authorities in Europe and the U.S. have stepped up pressure on providers to weed out unwanted content from cyberspace.

In one of the most widely publicised cases, German child pornography investigators searched CompuServe's Munich offices last November and gave the company a list of news groups so hardcore as to be considered illegal.

CompuServe, the country's second-largest internet provider, responded by banning access to some news groups and introducing software to filter out offending pages, drawing severe criticism from free speech advocates.
Austrian authorities have borrowed the German approach, and claim that providers are fully liable for illegal material that is fed into the net through their gateways.

"It is impossible to operate under such conditions," Rastl said. "Considering the sheer amount of information that is being made accessible on the net it is neither technically nor practically feasible to control the contents."

"This isn't about kicking off a no-censorship debate or rooting for having criminal content on the internet. What we want from the Austrian authorities is a clear legal basis for providing internet services," he added.
Internet providers maintain that their customers should be made responsible for whatever they put on the net and that they have set out clear and binding guidelines to that effect.

But the real problem, they say, is that authorities not just in Austria are still far too ignorant about the risks of cyberspace. ISPA now wants to offer Austrian investigators free computer training and unlimited access to the internet.
"This is a global problem which requires international solutions," Rastl said. "Unfortunately, the internet doesn't stop at borders, but political cooperation does."
